Decent citizens can no longer venture forth onto the streets, day or night, and even police officers are prime targets for murder and mayhem. Clearly something must be done. The answer as proposed in Jon Davison's production of RoboCop is a new breed of urban crimefighter - half man, half machine, all business. Engaged to create this cyborg superhero were film director Paul Verhoeven, actor Peter Weller and makeup effects artist Rob Bottin. Also contributing to the futuristic ambience were ED 209 creators Phil Tippett and Craig Davies, special photographic effects supervisor Peter Kuran, matte artist Rocco Gioffre and a host of others who discuss in detail their experiences on this most explosive of boxoffice hits. SHOOTING KOBOCOP article by Paul M. Sammon

"Basically, it's the story of a violent cyborg with an identity problem." That statement, by cowriter-coproducer Edward Neumeier, neatly encapsulates one of the year's biggest boxoffice hits - RoboCop- a high-impact blend of action, humor, science fiction and satire that has already racked up revenues in excess of $50 million. "RoboCop came out of a reaction to the later Eastwood and Bronson action pictures," Neumeier commented. "If Dirty Harry wanted to get a cup of coffee at a diner, then first he had to kill five guys to get it. The excessiveness of these films struck me as a kind of desperation, an indication of how ludicrous the genre was becoming. It also suggested the implicit humor in that excess." Collaborating on the script with Neumeier - himself a former studio reader and development executive - was Michael Miner, an experimental filmmaker who has worked extensively with director Alex Cox, shot numerous rock videos and recently directed his own screenplay, Deadly Weapon. "I always wanted RoboCop to be a movie that had its roots in comic books," Neumeier continued. "Just before we wrote the script, I had been reading a lot of comic books for a certain studio - and I had never really read them before. Particularly of this sort, which were of the modern neurotic superhero - Iron Man, Spider Man, Machine Man - the superhero that sort of had trouble being a superhero. Even though he had all these powers, there was something going on inside - he was a superhero with a headache. At the same time, there was a huge renaissance of adult comics going on. Suddenly there were all of these young artists producing their own books that were very mature, very driven kind of comics. And they weren't for kids anymore. Discovering that, I thought, 'Gee, we should do a moviel' - because comics books are a lot like movies." When their screenplay was finished, Neumeier and Miner took it to director Jonathan Kaplan who expressed enthusiasm for the project. The next step was to find an appropriate producer. At the top of the list was Jon Davison, a New York University alumnus and classmate of Kaplan who had spent his spare time in college operating the St. Marks Cinematheque repertory movie house and organizing film retrospectives at New York's legendary rock palace, the Fillmore East. Davison had first moved to Los Angeles to help rewrite the script for Kaplan's Night Call - a Roger Corman production - eventually moving up to a post as New World Pictures' director of national advertising and publicity. "Not long after I had bought the RoboCop script," Davison recalled, "Jonathan Kaplan was offered Project X at Fox. He took it, which left me without a director. There then followed a long process of talking to many people around town, but everyone was turning us down. Finally, someone suggested the Dutch director Paul Verhoeven. I had seen Paul's work since Turkish Delight and was a big fan of his Soldier of Orange and Spetters and The Fourth Man. In fact, Paul and I even had a couple of meetings regarding another project, an adaptation of Charles Bukowski's Women. But I never expected him to take on a film like RoboCop. When he did, frankly, I was a bit shocked." Although Verhoeven had initially turned down the project, a second reading of the RoboCop script convinced him that the story had merits beyond its action formula. Director in hand, Davison now cast Peter Weller - a cult favorite for his performance in The Adventures of Buckaroo Banzai - in the lead role of police officer Alex J. Murphy, an ordinary cop who is executed by a vicious gang of street criminals, then transformed into a near-indestructible crimefighter. To prepare for the role, Weller assidously spent four months training with the New York-based mime Moni Yakim in order to properly convey the movements of a very tough, but somewhat confused cyborg attempting to deal with big city crime while striving to regain some semblance of his former humanity. One crucial ingredient yet remained - assembling the film's special effects team. "I really do love robots," said Davison. "Who couldn't love Gort or Robby or Maria from Metropolis - or even interesting side-trips like The Colossus of New York? One of my earliest memories of robots is sitting in front of the television set as a four-year-old, watching a local Philadelphia show called Mr. Rivets - which was a man in a cardboard box painted silver. Hopefully on RoboCop we were going to do better than that. So to make sure Robo would be one of the most striking, most exciting robots ever filmed, we hired an allstar team of special effects people." RoboCop begins with a nighttime aerial shot of Detroit, where the futuristic story takes place. Although the metropolis seen in this flyover is indeed the home of Motown and General Motors, it is the only time Detroit actually appears in the film. "The opening scene is a stock shot of Detroit," Davison affirmed, "the only film stock shot in the entire picture. We had scouted Detroit as a possible location - after all, the movie takes place there - but its architecture just wasn't right." "RoboCop takes place in a slightly futuristic time," elaborated production designer William Sandell, "and details two separate environments which you ultimately discover are interlocking elements - the seedy underbelly of urban crime and the high-tech ivory towers of corporate life. So convincing locations were really critical to the story. For Murphy's death scene and RoboCop's climactic shootout, however, locations were needed that were not readily available in Texas. To this end, after principal photography in Dallas - which ran from early August to late October 1986 - the RoboCop production crew moved to an abandoned steel mill in the southwest Pennsylvania town of Monessen. Superimposed over the initial Detroit flyover is the film's first special effect - a glittering RoboCop logo. This burnished steel graphic was the work of special photographic effects supervisor Peter Kuran - a former ILM animator and subsequent founder of Visual Concept Engineering. In addition to providing select animation and opticals for Dragonslayer, Conan the Barbarian and Star Trek II, VCE also supplied all the visual effects for Dreamscape and contributed to two previous Jon Davison productions, Piranha and Airplane/ Working on RoboCop meant that VCE and Kuran would supply approximately eighty-five composites for the film, beginning with the logo. "The logo was done as a motion control shot," Kuran explained. "It began with a sketch I got from Orion Pictures, who released the film. It was just a little black-and-white thing showing the basic design of the letters themselves. Jon Davison wanted me to fudge with it and come up with something a little more striking. So we blew that logo up to a piece of backlit art about two feet long and five inches high, shading it with the gunmetal blues and grays you see in the film. "Shooting that art required one pass on our motion control system. Then another pass was needed to give the logo its metallic appearance. That pass employed a piece of eighth-inch aluminum plate which I brushed with sandpaper to give it detail and then set up on the rig - just a flat piece of metal that was large enough to cover side-to-side and top-to-bottom the same area as the artwork had. I lit that metal so that our camera picked up a lot of nice reflective detail on its surface and then shot it as yet another pass on the motion control. So by now we had a pass for the highlights, a pass for the whole letters - which later became the matte for the area the logo supered in over the Detroit background - and a pass for the gray unlit surface area of the metal. The surface which delineated the metal was later bipacked with the metal highlights so that it matted in the metal just on the surface of the letters, giving it that glittering metallic effect." Designed for maximum dramatic impact, the RoboCop logo zooms in from a distance until it nearly fills the screen. "Even though the travel on our motion control unit is fairly long," Kuran continued, "and even though I used a wide lens, the title zoom-in had to be done in two pieces. On most systems, it's just an impossibility to bring something in from infinity to where it fills the screen in a single shot. You simply don't have enough travel on your rig. So to get our two pieces, we started the logo out small and moved it up to the point where it rested at what would be considered one-to-one size. Then, after it held for a beat, we switched to a new setup with a longer lens and moved in from that point on." After the logo fills the screen, the letters are briefly filled with static 'snow' before the image cuts to the first of RoboCop's many 'MediaBreaks' - satirical newscasts of the future which punctuate the film and comment on its action. This logo static was obtained by shooting real video snow off a standard nineteen-inch monitor - done as a separate pass on the motion control unit, complete with slight move. Kuran then combined the static in VCE's optical printer as yet another element of the overall logo effect. The MediaBreaks feature two twinkling announcers who not only update the viewer on the latest armed insurrections in Acapulco, but also proffer a constant barrage of commercials for such products as artificial hearts and nuclear boardgames. Indeed, RoboCop is loaded with video imagery spotlighting commercials, newscasts and video-generated graphics and art - a conscious attempt on the part of the filmmakers to depict the Detroit of an unspecified future. In overall charge of RoboCop's various video sequences was Peter Conn of Homer and Associates, a Los Angeles firm which has done music videos, titles and computer graphics, plus a lot of television and film work. Conn's RoboCop tenure began when Davison contacted a mutual director friend, Rene Daalder, to ask if there was someone who could supervise the production of specific video graphics - namely video maps and readouts which would be seen on monitors inside the Detroit Police turbocruisers. Although the high-powered pursuit vehicles - actually redetailed Ford Tauruses - were indeed featured in the film, by the time principal photography commenced it was decided to shoot only their exteriors. By then, however, the interior video graphics had already been completed. "Jon and I met a couple of times," Conn recalled, "and then Paul Verhoeven came over and we talked about what they wanted to see. We did a whole bunch of police screens and we did mug shots, fingerprints, all kinds of generic police stuff for the car and for the police station. And for all that work, only one little piece made it into the film. That was in the scene when Murphy first enters the police locker room and you see this little monitor up on top of a locker reading off one of our visuals." Despite his original work not appearing in the film, Conn soon found himself taking on more and more RoboCop video chores until he was, in essence, filling the position of "Give us three minutes - we'll give you the world!" The opening proclamation from the MediaBreak quickly dissolves into a snowstorm of treated images as a number of 'video leaves' containing the smiling faces of news anchors Jesse Perkins (Entertainment Tonight's Leeza Gibbons) and Casey Wong (Mario Machado) separate and curl across the screen like petals on a windstorm. "I built that opening newsroom scene where

all the images fly in," Conn related. "But of course, before we could treat those images, we had to shoot the newscasts themselves - which we did at a place in Los Angeles called American Video Factory. All the MediaBreaks were shot in Betacam and then edited in component at Visual Eyes, which is a facility in Santa Monica. That material was then transferred to film directly from the component Betacam edit master. Component is a halfinch format - usually Betacam, although there are other ones - where the chrominance and the luminance signals are separate, thus giving you access to the colors directly before the video material is turned into an NTSC signal for normal recording and broadcast purposes. So by shooting in component and staying in component all the way, there was never any reason to introduce NTSC and coding and all the little artifacts that come along with it. "Once we had our video of the newscasters, Jim Rodnunsky and I were able to go in and get that flying image effect. Jim was video editor on RoboCop and had a lot of input into these areas. The flying images were all done with an ADO and an Abekas. An ADO is a common video device used for moving things around in the video screen. An Abekas is a digital disk recorder - also called a DDR - which allows you to go as many generations as you want in digital without losing definition or quality. So you can build one screen and then move on and build the next screen and the next one and the next one, and you're still only one generation down. That's how we did the opening. I think we had twenty-five screens in that sequence, though you barely see the outside ones in the 1.85 projection ratio. After a lot of planning, that was all done in one day." During the initial MediaBreak, the futuristic world of RoboCop is introduced via footage of a by-now functioning Star Wars defense system represented by video stock footage taken from a Public Broadcasting System documentary on the Strategic Defense Initiative. We are also introduced to the smarmy joys of Yamaha's new artificial heart. But viewers just as quickly learn that a cancer is eating at the heart of Old Detroit - the cancer of crime. Someone is killing dozens of policemen - and worse, no one seems to know why. Cut to one of those policemen, the aforementioned Murphy who has recently been reassigned to the Old Detroit precinct. In this battle-hardened environment, guardians of the law carry high-tech armament and wear futuristic body armor - actually available, off-the-shelf protection obtained from a company named SWAT Viper. No longer a public institution, the police department is run on a contract basis by OmniConsumer Products - a vast multinational conglomerate headquartered in a towering skyscraper safely outside the inner city combat zone. The literal basis for OCP's corporate headquarters was the ultramodern Dallas City Hall designed by famed architect I.M. Pei - 'literal basis' because the actual structure was deemed too small to serve RoboCop's purposes and now exists on film only as the six-story foundation of a seventy-story structure rendered by matte painter Rocco Gioffre. Seven matte paintings grace the film - all but one of which were done by Gioffre who also produced paintings for Close Encounters of the Third Kind, Star Trek - The Motion Picture, Gremlins, The Adventures of Buckaroo Banzai and Twilight Zone - The Movie. A founding partner of Dream Quest, Gioffre left that burgeoning organization in 1986 to form his own company offering not only matte painting work but stop-motion effects as well. "The usual technique that I employ," said Gioffre, "is original negative compositing. This involves going on location with a camera crew, very sturdily locking off your camera and then masking off the portion of the frame which will later be replaced with the painted artwork. On RoboCop, the paintings themselves were about thirty by forty inches in size - which is about the norm for a locked-off shot. They were done on masonite, my preference over glass. Glass is a bit heavier than masonite - and if you drop a glass matte, there's not only a danger of injury but more chance that you'll also lose your whole painting, If you drop masonite, you might scratch your painting - but that's it. Usually I do my paintings in oil. Every once in a while I'll do some work in acrylics, like an underpainting; but primarily I prefer brush painting and oils - no airbrushing or anything like that." In addition to the exterior shots, a number of matte paintings were employed to depict the interior of the OCP building where glass elevators silently ascend and descend above a busy central atrium composed of stairwells and plazas. "The trickiest shots on RoboCop were the down elevator angles," Gioffre resumed. "The plate photography on that was done in the interior of the Plaza of the Americas in Dallas. To do my masking, I had to shimmy out on a diving board type thing about five stories up, because the camera dolly was pushed out over the edge of a balcony and we were looking straight down. Of course, once I matted in the painting around that footage, it looked like it was closer to eighty stories down." It is during the first elevator scene that the audience is introduced to Bob Morton (Miguel Ferrer), a ruthless young executive who will soon be the major catalyst in the RoboCop construction process. "Although most of the matte shots were original negative, the two angles of Morton in the glass elevator - up and down - are actually dupe shots because we needed to get a much wider angle than we could accomplish with the lenses that we had on our plate camera. Ultimately, those were done as reduction dupes. In other words, the live-action photography was taken and placed in an optical printer and reduced by about fifty percent to fit into the painting. Ute Leonhardt at Praxis Film Works - Robbie Blalack's company - did the reduction dupes on that. Then I took those and comped them with the paintings at my own facility. For the live-action element of the glass elevator shots we primarily used just one small circular staircase and one walking path at the Plaza of the Americas. The Plaza also has about four elevator shafts; but we really couldn't use them due to their locations, so we shot only one of those shafts ourselves. Gioffre assumed about half of the compositing chores of the live-action and matte painting elements at his own facility, while passing on the remaining comps to Michael Karp and Don Baker at Praxis. Morton's elevator deposits him in the OCP executive boardroom, a location set built on the fifty-seventh floor of Dallas' Renaissance Tower. (Most of the film's other interiors were erected within Las Colinas, a local Dallas soundstage facility.) Once inside, Morton and the other corporate executives are treated to a briefing by Security Concepts vice president Dick Jones (Ronny Cox). The presentation begins with a multi-video array fed through a literal wall of monitors, all detailing the ted through a pe endless areas in which OCP has stuck its greedy corporate fingers. "Originally there were going to be a great many more video monitors scattered around RoboCop," commented Jon Davison. "It's something that Paul Verhoeven wanted to do a lot of. But I tried to convince him in preproduction that monitors in the background of every shot were ultimately going to take more time than they were worth. So Paul sort of simplified that after awhile - but he certainly got his monitors during the boardroom sequence." More than two dozen Proton monitors were employed on the set, with imagery played back on a battery of three-quarter-inch tape machines handled by video technician Jeff Santlofer. Although the 'video wall' behind Jones seems alive with separate shots during the sequence, the images are actually repeated segments from only a dozen stock video featurettes constantly being recycled to different monitors at different times. This video stock footage was supplied in part by Intervideo, a company which also provided the playback units and monitors for the sequence. Animated titles superimposed over the images were generated by Peter Conn. Surprisingly, the briefing sequence was shot without video interlock, a system which reduces video from its normal thirty frames per second down to a motion picture compatible twenty-four frames per second. "We didn't use synchronized playback because frankly we didn't have the money," explained Davison. "So we just let the playback units run on in thirty-frame video and adjusted the shutter in our camera to get rid of the roll bar. Except for one sequence - Murphy in the Compulab -we never did interlock." The purpose of Dick Jones' presentation is to announce OCP's embarkation on the Delta City project - a gigantic urban redevelopment complex targeted for the very heart of Old Detroit. Gesturing toward the architectural model spread out near the central conference table - a model constructed under the supervision of art director Gayle Simon - Jones stresses that before work on Delta City can commence, the wave of rampant crime sweeping Old Detroit must first be stopped. Dramatically, Jones then ushers in his division's new automated security robot - Enforcement Droid 209. Squat, powerful, only vaguely anthropomorphic, ED 209 is one of RoboCop's design and effects highlights - brought into being under the guiding hand of stop-motion animator Phil

Tippett, an Oscar winner for Return of the Jedi whose other credits include The Empire Strikes Back and Dragonslayer as well as the more recent Howard the Duck and The Golden Child. "Based on the Robocop script," said Tippett, "I had initially done some quick pencil sketches for Jon to help him budget out ED 209. Then, when Paul Verhoeven came on board, we sat down for hours tearing that design apart. That's when I contacted Craig Davies. If there's any single person responsible for the design and construction of ED 209, it's Craig." A San Francisco Bay Area resident who had previously built props for body for a nt props for rock videos - also an articulated duck body for a never-used Howard the Duck puppet - Davies was initially approached by Tippett while working on tactical fighter helmets for an elecпорені на ох tronics company. Intrigued by Tippett's proposal that he become involved in the ED 209 project, Davies flew down to Los Angeles to meet with Paul Verhoeven and Jon Davison. "When Paul and I began discussing the design of ED 209," Tippett continued, "one of the things we realized we had going for us was that ED is a machine. It was also decided that the liveaction ED 209 - a full-size prop - would be more or less used as a static object that the actors could relate to directly during principal photography. Any actual movement or fighting on ED's part would be done in stop-motion. Those were the parameters Craig had to work with." "Paul Verhoeven made it immediately clear that he didn't want anything on ED 209 to look cute," Davies elaborated. "He wanted something really hard and mean. Verhoeven had a really severe vision in mind for this thing. I myself already had a pretty strong idea of what a giant robot should look like, especially when it was a product of modern American design. To begin, I thought it wouldn't be designed to be wholly functional. First they'd design it to look neat and then they'd worry about making it work. In other words, these futuristic designers would pay a lot of attention to the cosmetics of it in an attempt to market the thing on looks alone - just like an American car." "With Verhoeven's help," said Tippett, "Craig designed ED 209 to be very industrial looking. Initially, the design was going to be something very quick and easy. But Paul Verhoeven was very insistent that the robot have a killer look and that it not have a face. And all the design work we were coming up with was just too innocuous - you couldn't really tell what you were looking at. So Craig came up with the idea of making a killer whale face. We made an air intake on the central pod - which basically added a face to it and gave ED the expression of having a mouth whose lips were locked in a death grimace. Then Craig loosely designed the coloring around a killer whale's - black on the top, with lighter tones on the bottom." "Actually," said Davies, "the design is like a killer whale mixed with a U.S. Air Force Corsair jet. These things fly over the San Francisco Bay Bridge, and a couple of times I've seen them emerge out of the fog and fly - VAROOMMI - fifty feet above me. Whenever they do that, it scares the shit out of me. So that's a really strong element. I also took a lot of the current design trends into account and mixed them all together, adding things like oil coolers, radiators and heat exchangers, all of which are on that robot if you know where to look. Of course, the question of eyes came up, but I thought it was best to avoid them. Eyes have too much emotion in them, first of all; and secondly, robotic eyes have become a big cliche. So I got away from that idea. I did, however, include things that were my own digs at what I see as a really lame current corporate design policy. for instance, there are four huge hydraulic rams on the legs, even though a creature like ED wouldn't need nearly that many. So it's like complete redundancy - a true corporate product. Also there's the grill area in ED's head. Some people look at that and they go, 'Oh, it's a mouth.' But it's also a big, obvious, extremely stupid place to put an open area like a radiator on a fighting unit like ED 209. Through those kinds of things my feelings about the real Detroit come through on the robot." Working in the San Rafael workshop of Peter Ronzani - assisted by Paula Lucchesi who made all the fiberglass and urethane molds and also did about half of the body work - Davies began assembling the full-scale ED 209. "First I built a small-scale model - about eight inches tall - out of foam and foamcore and various pieces of plastic. From that model I broke ED down into small 3-D drawings with some of his actual working geometry, added little working hydraulic systems and basically just figured out the whole thing on paper. After that we took the model, made a mold of it and band-sawed that up into half-inch-thick sections like you would a loaf of broad. Each of those cross-sections was sketched out on a piece of graph paper and then enlarged to proper scale on a wall with an opaque projector. Having figured out our full scale this way, we then put the pieces back on paper and transferred the various shapes onto wood. By putting all our wooden cross-sections together, we now had a full-scale 3-D mockup. For the compound curves - especially on the head - we used strips of pine cut to a sixteenth-of-an-inch thick so that they would conform to these compound curves without buckling. We then took that shape and put fiberglass and papier-mache over it to form a solid surface, bondoing it to get it real smooth. For all the ED 209 sections that were relatively flat or had only a few degrees in curvature, we used pieces of masonite ripped up to the right shape by the band saw. We primed each part and got it all together making sure that things like the arms and legs were to be vacuformed. "All the main body parts on the full-scale ED 209 - the head, the arms, the legs and midsection - were fiberglass. All the detailed parts were vacuformed. So it was entirely plastic. The only metal we used were the screws holding the wooden underframe together. Finished it stood seven feet tall and weighed in at about three hundred pounds. And it took four months of really exhausting work to build. Because the relationship between Jack and Tuck was the film's primary focus, the special effects, though obligatory, were intended as a means to an end rather than the film's reason for being. With this in mind, Dante and company turned to visual effects supervisor Dennis Muren and Industrial Light and Magic. "Effects-wise," said Dante, "our number one priority was to try to not make it look like Fantastic Voyage, because the idea of remaking a picture has never appealed to me and I knew we were already going to be in trouble because both films have the same premise. Fantastic Voyage, however, is much more stylized than would be permissible today where realism seems to be the name of the game. Knowing this, we tried to have it both ways. We tried to make Innerspace realistic enough to be convincing, but stylized enough to not be disgusting since there are a lot of people who find it difficult to look at things like gooey body parts. This is where ILM really came in because we were able to maintain that balance throughout the film. We made a decision early on not to make it a 'special effects spectacular' - because that really isn't what the picture is about. I think one of the flaws of Fantastic Voyage is that an inordinate amount of time is spent gawking at the special effects. We tried to make the effects for Innerspace as functional as they would be if the story weren't taking place inside the body - as if Tuck were in a car somewhere instead of inside Jack Putter. In keeping with the film's general avoidance of opticals, the dauntless pair were rendered pint-size by means of oversize set pieces and forced perspective photography. "The forced perspective material was not in the original script," said Joe Dante. "But we thought we needed to do more with the miniaturization idea, so we decided to shrink the 66 • CINEFEX 32 TELEPH NE

villains to half size - and there was some concern about how we were going to do it. Obviously they had to interact with the other live actors. Bluescreen didn't seem to be quite the way to do it; and while I had thought about the idea of forced perspective, I simply thought it would be too hard. I ran Darby O'Gill and the Little People and remembered the hardships they went through while making the picture and just figured it would be too complicated for Innerspace. But Dennis Muren had great faith in the idea of doing forced perspective. He is very learned in nodal points and all that other kind of stuff you have to know. Of course, there were certain inherent problems. The sequence included a car which was supposed to be moving very fast, and there was a lot of action and interaction between the two figures in the back seat with the two figures in the front seat - and the camera had to simulate motion. Now if you get off your nodal point, the gimmick - that the people in front are close and the people in back are farther off - is given away. So it was very tricky and it took quite a bit of trial and error - and a great deal of footage. We shot almost a week on that sequence just to get the best possible pieces. The outtakes were hilarious. The actors had to look at monitors to see what it was that they were doing; so if one actor had to put his hand up in the rear while another actor had to put his hand up in the front to look like they're touching, the only way they could seem to connect was by watching a monitor to see where their hands had to go. It was extremely difficult work, but it was lots of fun because Kevin McCarthy is a riot and Martin Short is hysterical; and what could have been a really tedious process was made quite bearable because the actors were so game." "I had experience doing forced perspective with some commercials I'd worked on," recalled Dennis Muren, "but Innerspace was the first time it's come up in a film where there were enough shots in one location to build essentially one set and make it work economically. We really didn't want to do the car chase sequence bluescreen. We would have had problems because of everything having to be locked off, and creating mattes would have been very difficult. It just seemed like a good opportunity to try something with forced perspective because it was a setup already - you have these miniature characters in the back seat and these bigger characters in the front seat. It was simply a matter of letting it all out. At first, however, there was a lot of question as to how we could actually make it work. So I made a little model of the setup to make it clear to Joe and the art director, and they got ideas and it became a real exciting prospect. We were able to do the shots and have the performances right there on the set - which was best for the actors, best for Joe and best for the cameraman, Andy Laszlo, who could see it and light it in its finished form. Although the finalized version of Innerspace ends with a parting shot of the miniaturized villains in the trunk of Tuck's car, a substantial amount of fully realized effects footage was deleted as the film progressed through postproduction. "One nice thing about ILM is that you never hear them grousing about the great shot that didn't get in the picture," commented Joe Dante. "At least I never heard them. We knew in the beginning that there would be certain set pieces in the movie - the heart scene, the stomach, the eyeball, the ear - but for the most part it wasn't really established where Tuck was at any given time and it wasn't really very interesting where he was. ILM did a lot of those kinds of shots - which we called generic shots - just to remind people that he was inside the body. But when we went to cut the picture together, we discovered that the relationship between Martin Short and Dennis Quaid was so important to the movie that you wanted to see Dennis' face a lot more. So places where we'd planned to put shots of the pod traveling through some interesting background and you'd just hear Dennis' voice simply weren't as good that way. You wanted to see what he was thinking and what his reaction was. As a result there were a number of sequences in the picture which were originally planned to have ILM shots that ended up as cutto-closeups of these two guys talking, But it was that personal element of the film that I found most appealing - that and the opportunity to do something a little bit different. For me, there is nothing more deadening than the thought of having to make the same sort of picture over and over again - which is why I haven't directed sequels to any of my films. Quite simply, Innerspace was a kind of movie I had never done before - and it had a lot more emphasis on characterization, which I liked a lot. Someone told me they thought this was a 'transitional work' for me — but frankly, I don't know what any of that stuff means. To me, what it offered was a chance to try something new and interesting. Beyond that, I just try to do whatever's right for the movie."
